item.title: Percent-encode userinfo in `database::userinfo` — raw `/`, `?`, `#` in a password break connections and defeat redaction

issues.title: Percent-encode userinfo in `database::userinfo` — raw `/`, `?`, `#` in a password break connections and defeat redaction
issues.body:
Follow-up from Holmes's review of #355 (PR #358).

**Observation:** `database::userinfo` splices the `.env` password into a connection URL with no percent-encoding:

```rust
format!("{user}:{password}")   // laravel-lsp/src/database.rs:468-473
```

RFC 3986 requires `@`, `/`, `?` and `#` in a userinfo component to be percent-encoded. Not doing so causes two distinct failures, one functional and one a credential-disclosure hazard.

**1. Connections silently fail.** `sqlx` parses connection strings through `Url::parse` (`sqlx-mysql-0.9.0/src/options/parse.rs:91`). A password containing `/` makes `build_mysql_candidates` manufacture `mysql://user:p/ss@host:3306/db`, which the parser rejects with *invalid port number* — schema introspection fails with no useful diagnostic.

**2. The redaction gate fails open on the same class.** PR #358 rewrote `mask_url_credentials` to decide the credential span with an RFC 3986 parse. That closed the `@`-in-password leak (#355) and the path-`@` mangling, but one class survives: a password whose leading run up to a raw `/`, `?` or `#` is entirely ASCII digits ≤ 65535. The parser reads `user:<digits>` as `host:port`, reports no password, and the value is returned **completely unmasked** across all four display surfaces plus the server log. Verified by compiling PR #358's exact function body against `url` 2.5.8:

```
mysql://user:12/34@host/db                | parse ok, password=None | out: mysql://user:12/34@host/db
mysql://user:1234/56@host/db              | parse ok, password=None | out: mysql://user:1234/56@host/db
mysql://user:012345/aG9zdG5hbWU=@host/db  | parse ok, password=None | out: mysql://user:012345/aG9zdG5hbWU=@host/db
```

The third line is the one that matters: `openssl rand -base64` output contains `/` and digits, so this is a plausible generated-password shape rather than an exotic one.

**Why this can't be fixed in `mask_url_credentials`:** `mysql://user:12/34@host/db` and `mysql://host:3306/db@x` are structurally identical to any RFC 3986 parser — valid host, valid port, path containing `@`. No rule inside the masking function separates them, and #355's AC explicitly requires the latter to come back untouched. PR #358 documents this residue accurately and pins it with a test; it is genuinely irreducible at that layer.

Percent-encoding at the point of construction is the fix that actually retires the class. Every URL the LSP builds would then parse cleanly, `password()` would always be `Some`, and the fail-open arm would be unreachable for anything this codebase produces.

**Location:** `laravel-lsp/src/database.rs:468-473` (`userinfo`), with call sites in `build_mysql_candidates` and `build_postgres_candidates` (`:2237`).

**Tracked under:** latent-hazard

Non-blocking, and *unrelated to the coherent unit PR #358 delivers* — #358 is a display-layer redaction fix and closes its own class correctly. This is a connection-string defect whose repair happens to also eliminate the display residue. It belongs to whoever picks up `userinfo()`, not to #355.

Note that a `.env` value a **user** types with a raw `/` in the password is outside this fix's reach and stays in the documented fail-open set — but such a value is already non-functional as a connection string for Laravel itself, so the practical exposure after this change is close to nil.

<!-- followup-from: PR#358 -->

held_acceptance_criteria:
<!-- acceptance-criteria -->

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `database::userinfo()` (laravel-lsp/src/database.rs:468) percent-encodes every byte not in RFC 3986's `unreserved` (`ALPHA DIGIT - . _ ~`) or `sub-delims` (`! $ & ' ( ) * + , ; =`) set — this includes `:`, `/`, `?`, `#`, `[`, `]`, `@`, `%`, space, control bytes, and non-ASCII UTF-8 bytes. Applies identically to **both** the username and the password. A literal `:` in the *username* is encoded too, even though RFC 3986's general userinfo grammar permits it unencoded — this function uses `:` as its own username/password separator, so an unencoded `:` there mis-splits the same way the digit-run/`/` collision mis-splits a password.
- [ ] All four call sites that build a URL through `userinfo()` receive the encoded value: `build_mysql_candidates`'s unix-socket and TCP branches, and `build_postgres_candidates`'s unix-socket and TCP branches. No caller is left splicing a raw, unencoded credential.
- [ ] A password containing `/`, `?`, `#`, or `@` (e.g. an `openssl rand -base64`-shaped value, matching the issue's examples) now parses successfully via `sqlx::mysql::MySqlConnectOptions` / `sqlx::postgres::PgConnectOptions`'s `FromStr` (already a dependency — no new crate needed), yielding the intended username and password through their accessors — not a parse error, and not a misread host/port for the digit-run cases.
- [ ] A credential built only from legal `unreserved`/`sub-delims` characters (including marks like `!$&'()*+,;=~-._`) produces a byte-for-byte identical URL to today's output — no incidental re-encoding of already-safe or already-legal characters. The empty-password no-trailing-colon behavior (`mysql://root@host/db`, never `mysql://root:@host/db`) is preserved.
- [ ] A literal `%` in a credential is always percent-encoded to `%25`, with no ambiguity: a password containing `%` immediately followed by two hex digits (e.g. `sec%3Dret`) round-trips to the literal string `sec%3Dret`, never decoding to `sec=ret`.
- [ ] The `DB_URL` passthrough candidate (`config.url`, both MySQL and Postgres) is untouched — encoding applies only to URLs `userinfo()` helps construct, never to a full connection string supplied verbatim by the user.
- [ ] Unit tests, each verified via the `MySqlConnectOptions`/`PgConnectOptions` parse named above, cover: (a) a password containing `/`, one containing `?`, one containing `#`, one containing `@`; (b) the digit-run-before-`/` shapes quoted in the issue (`12/34`, `1234/56`, `012345/aG9zdG5hbWU=`) plus the equivalent digit-run-before-`?` and digit-run-before-`#` shapes (e.g. `12?34`, `12#34`); (c) a username containing a reserved character (e.g. `foo@bar` or `a:b`), proving the username is encoded symmetrically with the password; (d) at least one test per production call site — both branches of `build_mysql_candidates` and both branches of `build_postgres_candidates` — building a real `ConnCandidate` with a special-character credential and confirming the credential *and* the trailing `socket=`/`host=` query value both parse back correctly.
